utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This afternoon we are starting the cross-examination. Who is beginning, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. And good afternoon to everyone, all the participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that you have had a rest and that you are ready to continue answering the questions. I will not take too much time asking you questions but what I will want to do is to clarify some things that you have already mentioned about during your examination-in-chief and that are interesting for me with respect to the defence of my client. What I recalled is that on the first day of the testimony, that was on the 6th of May, you described a meeting in Prud on the 19th of March, 1992, and then you mentioned to Mr. Pisarevic, you mentioned Mr. Blazanovic, Braco, you mentioned him, he was a member of the Croatian Army and that he was active when attending that meeting. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already heard his name several times during the testimony of other witnesses and during the Prosecution case, some witnesses mentioned him and I thought this was interesting also -- he was also mentioned in the Defence case and some persons you mentioned -- mentioned him. Now, bearing in mind the work you did before the war and during the war, more in particular your intelligence information and what you've heard here in the courtroom regarding the testimonies of the witnesses who testified about him, do you have any knowledge that he organised the bringing out of certain people from the municipality of Samac in the beginning of the conflict, a number of people from which villages and so on? Do you know anything about it? Particularly, did you know -- did you have any personal knowledge of that happening during at that period of time? Did you have any contemporaneous knowledge of those facts?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had some intelligence information which pointed to the presence of Mr. Blazanovic, Stjepan Blazanovic, also known as Braco, precisely in the territory of the municipality of Samac, and in particular, in that part of the municipality that those parts that were populated with Croatian populations and I mean Donji and Gornji Hasici, part of the Croatian Tisina and part of Novo Selo so approximately this is where his activities took place, and it was by him coming on to the terrain and with a number of people who were with him, together with him, he managed, after the war broke out, after the conflict broke out, he managed to extract a relatively large number of Croatian citizens to safely take them out to that part of the territory which according to him was the safest part of the territory so that they could go in the direction of Grebnice, Domaljevac, Bazik, or more precisely, to that part of the municipality of Samac where there were mostly Croats or exclusively Croats living at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this Court, we heard that he managed to take out about 250 people, villagers from those villages. After the departure of women and children -- mostly women and children, do you remember we heard that in closed session but what I'm interested is this what your information is regarding the number of people that he managed to take out?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Precisely, yes, this corresponds to this information. We always thought that this was a couple of hundred people of Croat nationals, mostly women and children, that he managed to take out, taking them into the direction that I mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also heard the testimony of my client and some other witnesses that at the time there was the attack on the bus of Serb soldiers who were going towards the front line. Do you have any knowledge regarding this? Is this something that you know about? Was this at that time about mid-May as it was alleged?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know about that event, in particular, because at the time, I was deputy commander for security of the 4th Detachment and part of the people, precisely from Samac, used a specific direction to move into the new then defence positions that were gravitating towards the main road, which links Samac to Obudovac and it cuts off practically part of the territory which further goes towards Croatian villages, Grebnice, Bazik and Domaljevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown a map, and perhaps he could draw this location where the attack on the bus happened, and I would like us to use the map we've already used in this case, and this is the map from the expert report of Mrs. Tabeau but now this is a map from the work of Mrs. Radovanovic because it is slightly changed in the B/C/S version but it is very clear and it would be good to show it and I would like to ask some questions, so I would ask Mr. Usher to show the map to the witness, to put it in front of the witness. Thank you. What I need is, if you can draw and mark with number 1 where was the location of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And also where was the line which was then the demarcation line, the line between the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: First of all I'd like to draw a line, the itinerary of the bus which at that time it was going as a regular bus taking the soldiers, taking them to the positions, and then approximately, in my opinion, I could put where the location is, because the map doesn't have too many details so I cannot be absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well, if you can do that, that's even better.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: From the town of Samac, there was this road, and then here it goes left towards Tisina, through Tisina, the bus went along this road to Novo Selo, and then from Novo Selo, approximately it would take this route that I am drawing now. It would come to as I would call it, this regional road, this is the one I'm pointing to with the pen, which connected Bosanski Samac to the depth of the territory and it was going further towards Obudovac. This incident that took place and that I mentioned earlier, it happened approximately here, right in the middle of Novo Selo, where there were not so many populated houses and then it continued, the settlement of Novo Selo continues and then it went to -- the road went on to Brvnik where there were our Defence lines which were undulating and following this direction, along the Sava River and then again, practically along the embankment return to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zaric, so that we can have the drawing clear for later, could you just put it in a dotted line so that we can see that it's a different -- that the defence line should be different from the route of the bus, or make it thicker, but so that we have to differentiate between these two lines?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: What I'm doing now, that's approximately the defence line, which was behind the regional road which connects municipality of Samac to the depth of the territory towards Obudovac but from there, this is practically the route of this bus, while this dot here, which is slightly more marked, more pronounced, this is where the bus was ambushed, which I think happened on the 12th or the 13th of May, I'm not quite sure about the date but approximately that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment. I'd like you to mark number 1, the route, the itinerary of the bus?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With number 2, if you can mark the location of the incident where the attack on the bus happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And with number 3, could you please mark the demarcation line between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that according to your recollection, that happened on the 12th or the 13th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on the 12th or the 13th of May, and it was a bus of soldiers that was going in that direction, and to be honest, according to my recollection, that bus, apart from the people who were from Samac mostly, predominantly, there were many people who were originally and who were engaged but who were originally from Donja Dubica and Novi Grad, and they had come to our area, that bus was practically ambushed in a classical sabotage terrorist way. It was riddled with bullets and I recall that the driver of the bus only thanks to him, his name is Mico Kuresevic, we called him Smokljo, that was his nickname, he was injured in several places, dozens of bullets went through his body but it was thanks to him and to his cool head, he managed to get the bus out in that direction -- in this direction, towards the line of the defence, and there, there were already some people from our area, and practically he managed to move the bus towards there, with many injured soldiers, some of them are -- have remained disabled, like a young man who to this date is now disabled in a wheelchair and many others have still some consequences -- serious consequences from this ambush which was set up in a classical way and which provoked a great degree of upset and those of us who led the army, among the people in the area of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this ambush was deep in the territory which at the time was under the control of the JNA so to speak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was deep in our territory, in the territory under our control, but it was thanks to Mr. Cepanovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Blazanovic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Stjepan Blazanovic, it was thanks to this instructor of the Croatian Army who was probably an expert, he was brave and courageous and he brought this group of people and they did what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I would just like to say is that for the record, under number 1, the witness marked the direction of the bus, of the route of the bus, the direction in which bus was going. Second was the location of the attack on the bus, and number 3 marks the front line which is a demarcation line between the warring sides. If there are no objections could we please have exhibit number for this exhibit? And if we can tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not object, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D195/3, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we are still on this subject, and you've also testified about your intelligence information regarding the pre-war arming, what I'm particularly interested in regarding these villages that we are talking about, and we know already, all of us here in the courtroom, we know that these are the villages that were populated with Croatian population, Donji Gornji Hasici, Novo Selo, and Zasavica, Brvnik. You mentioned a field gun that was in Hasici. I'm interested in after the war broke out, did you find out that the villagers of these villages were really armed, and what were their weapons? Do you know? First of all, could you answer that question and then I'll ask you something else but could you tell us about your intelligence information regarding the weapons and the arming in these villages when detentions took place, the villagers in those villages, were they really armed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It was not a field gun of a large calibre. It was a mortar, 120 millimetre mortar which according to my assessment is a very lethal weapon with a long range so we later found out, we got data, that these were 120 millimetre mortars and then through certain stories, we heard when they were searching them because it was on the 8th of February, allegedly the police was working investigating this case but nothing was found, that it was precisely that mortar they managed to get that mortar out in a barrel for brandy, they managed to get it out, but that happened later after the conflict broke out by some people in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you later find out, did you have later intelligence, that it was in this territory, in these villages, that a large amount of weapons were seized?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did know that, because there was an operation that was carried out, what was gathered, weapons were gathered, what was found were classical weapons that had belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, because there were automatic weapons, semi-automatic rifles and also old M-48 rifles and classical small automatic rifles of German and Russian manufacturer so it was after this operation, after the conflict broke out, in these Croatian villages, a large amount of weapons were seized and taken to the Territorial Defence warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified about a number of villagers from these villages who were taken to the secondary school and the primary school, did I understand from your testimony that you contacted Sarkanovic and Savic frequently, your colleagues, I shouldn't say colleagues but SUP inspectors that you knew, did they give you information that it was against -- that these people were investigated, that there were certain interviews that were conducted with these people? Did you have this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely on this theme, I found from Mr. Sarkanovic, who was the chief of the criminal department, and Mr. Savic [as interpreted], that after these people were placed in isolation in the hall of both schools, interviews were held with them on the topic of the possession of illegal weapons in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the trip, those words were actually said by -- in different order. The answer of Mr. Zaric on page 9, line 12 it says, "precisely on this theme, I found from Mr. Sarkanovic, who was the chief of the criminal department, and Mr. Savic," so words Mr. Savic were before who was the chief of the criminal department, because it is, I believe, not in dispute that Mr. Milos Savic was chief of the criminal investigation and Mr. Sarkanovic wan just an investigator in the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that will be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a slight suggestion from my colleagues, when you were mentioning this, what's the name, the mortar, 120 millimetre, is that the VBR, the multiple rocket launcher that's mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, 120 millimetre mortar is a classic artillery piece, it has different calibres with one barrel, it can be 120, 80 or 60 millimetres. As I was an artillery man in the army, I know this, and it is not contested that this is weapons which is not a VBR or not weapon which at the same time simultaneously can fire several rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Now I'm going to ask you some questions about the decision on the isolation of Croats that you've testified in -- that is P71. There is no need for this exhibit, this document, to be placed in front of you. I understood from your testimony that when you were describing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before you proceed and before we leave this topic of the attack on the bus, it is my understanding from your testimony, Mr. Zaric, that nobody was arrested for this attack on the bus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam President, nobody was arrested. We immediately organised part of our forces to try and discover who were the perpetrators but apart from the traces where they had been and in which direction they went, through which channel they managed to get out, at that time, it was -- there was a lot of greenery and it was quite clear from the grass where they had gone, we didn't manage to uncover any perpetrators who had done this, but it was in the evening and in the following few days, nonstop through the communications, that both sides used, they, I mean the Croatian side, they boasted how they had carried out this operation, and for us, this was uncontested. Nobody else except for a very well prepared and well-organised sabotage group could have done this, could have attacked a bus full of soldiers going to the position, to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about this decision regarding the isolation of Croats and regarding the written document that you've testified in chief when Mr. Pisarevic was asking you questions. From your testimony, I got an impression, perhaps you can tell me whether I was right, you told me that regarding this decision on isolation, you found out about it from two sources, one source was your direct ability to notice when Croats were taken away in lorries, from your neighbourhood, and the second source is also your direct knowledge, that is that the written document, P71, you were able to see in Mr. Todorovic's office and also in the offices of Mr. Sarkanovic and Mr. Savic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that decision, did you speak about it with any members of the Crisis Staff or rather did you find out about this decision being issued from any members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't speak to any members of the Crisis Staff, apart from seeing this decision on the desk of Mr. Todorovic and I saw it on the desk in a couple of copies, also in Mr. Savic's office and Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic's office who were investigators and I spoke about it to Mr. Savo Cancarevic, who had been the commander at that time of the police in Samac because I didn't find it normal, I didn't find it pleasant, because I had seen this scene that the police was rounding people up, putting them in lorries and that reminded me of a very, very ugly picture, and Savo told me that this was chief, Stevan Todorovic, had said that the police were supposed to do this, that there was a decision of the Crisis Staff regarding this, and this decision, when I saw it, when I saw it in front of me, at that very moment, I didn't even enter into any kind of legal matters, so to speak. How much is it an impression of some truth and authenticity but I saw the signature, I saw the -- what said on the top of the document and I could see that according to what I was able to observe, there was a signature of Mr. Blagoje Simic, as far as I can recall, and then I thought that what later happened, very quickly, people were collected in these two schools, people had gone to Zasavica and my normal conclusion I would say was that behind that decision Crisis Staff was behind this decision. Was standing behind that decision but to be absolutely honest regarding this topic apart from these people I did not speak to anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, did he ever tell you that this was a decision of the Crisis Staff? Did you ever speak to him about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I never spoke to Mr. Todorovic about this because I thought that it was unnecessary to speak to him about this since his police was doing some work on the streets and they were doing things which according to me were completely unacceptable, inhumane, I don't even have words to express it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic and Savic, those two gentlemen, did they tell you that they know that the Crisis Staff had brought this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. They said that Mr. Todorovic said that there was a decision from the Crisis Staff but they had not spoken to some of the people from that level, I don't know, meaning to say that this information was all based on what -- on the information that I received from Mr. Savic, being the chief of the criminal department, Mr. Vladimir Sarkanovic and from Mr. Savo Cancarevic, who had said that he does have the order from the chief of the police to engage the police in order to pick up the Croats and to bring them into isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would also like to know one thing regarding this decision, I suppose Mr. Zaric that before you surrendered to this Tribunal and especially when this trial began, I suppose that you had the possibility to speak with Mr. Tadic regarding this decision. Did Mr. Tadic ever tell you that he was aware of this decision in any of the conversations he had with you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, he never told me anything of the sort. We did speak about this. Now regarding this decision and his knowledge about it, Mr. Tadic never told me that he knew anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to talk about another topic, it is something that you've testified about regarding this first exchange that took place in Zasavica on the 26th of May. You've told us about it, about this event, you told us what happened, you told us also that you were about 30 metres away from the truck in which people were placed, people who were to be exchanged and that the place was from 300 to 400 metres away from the river. My question is the following: Do you recall where Tadic was at that point with regards to the place where you were, was he next to the truck, was he next to you, or maybe you didn't see him at all then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, during all that time, I must have seen him twice or three times in the part that goes from the trucks in the direction of the winding road that -- through which these people who were exchanged were going, in order to be exchanged, towards the River Bosna, there was a point there, and this is where the direct exchange was taking place, the exchange over the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Tadic call some names?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tadic did not call any names. The calling of names was carried out by a member of the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, and he was assisted by a police officer just in case that foreigner did not pronounce the names correctly, the police officer was helping him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard if Mr. Tadic at that time yelled at anybody?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that you must remember that at that point, Serbs came for the exchange but I would like to ask you the following question: Do you remember if all the Serbs who were to be exchanged, were they all exchanged? Do you know anything about this? Do you have any knowledge about their exchanges? Have you heard about this from anybody?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I have heard something about it when they arrived at the company Tekstilac, actually this is a restaurant, and there was a welcoming lunch for the representatives of the International Red Cross and these people had arrived on that side to say that way, and I had heard then from the conversation that there were -- there was about ten Serbs who were on the other side in the territory of the municipality of Odzak, they were supposed to cross but they did not, either because it was not allowed for them to do so or I don't know what the truth is, but there was a certain number of Croats and I don't know if some Muslims were part of that group, I'm not sure, but I know that a certain number of people on this side, as Mr. Petric was, he was not the only one, there were also others who said that they did not want to cross to the other side, they returned, and that is maybe why the agreement was not respected to exchange hundreds of people. And this is why a certain number of Serbs was returned or actually they did not even cross on the other side, and this is what people were saying, the people with whom we were having lunch, they were sitting there, we were talking to them and they knew who they were because they had arrived there with them together on the other bank of the river which was under the control of the HVO and the forces of the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions about the July exchanges. You have told us that you were present during those exchanges, you've also described to us problems that occurred during the bringing of Mr. Grga Zubak to that exchange. You have heard also my client testify before this Honourable Trial Chamber and he participated in the organisation of -- he organised this exchange. Mr. Todorovic was being treated after a medical -- he had an undergone medical treatment after an accident. Do you know if Savo Cancarevic and my client had any problems with Todorovic because Grga Zubak left then, this is what my client said and this is why he was transferred to do something else. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had received some information regarding this. Mr. Tadic and Mr. Cancarevic during some conversations told me that when Mr. Todorovic returned from the hospital after an accident, a car accident, which he was involved in, he was saying why was it allowed that Grga Zubak goes but I would like to say that at the checkpoint in Gorice, the chief of the private department police, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and they used to call each other Kum, and there was a man who did not allow Mr. Grga Zubak to be transported in a bus as a man who was to be exchanged, and this is when Mr. Tadic, I must be honest, they told this police officer that it was not his place to do so, it was a man who was extremely rough, and arrogant, he is an uncouth police officer and I believe that at the time he only wore a police uniform, only at that time, never again, and this is why I deem or I believe that when Mr. Cancarevic and Tadic told me about this problem and that problem escalated when Mr. Todorovic came back from the hospital, through Mr. Todorovic or according to Mr. Todorovic rather he was a person for whom they could get points through him. They were talking about this as if they were not talking about people but points, and I remember this very well. I also know that there was a physical brawl between Mr. Cancarevic and Todorovic after that, and this is a story that was circulating in the town of Samac, that the chief of the security station and the chief of police had an open fight on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I hope that Mr. Lukic will clarify certain parts of Mr. Zaric's answer because looking at it in the transcript, I find them -- well, not particularly clear. First of all, on page 16, here it says chief of the private department police, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and I don't believe this is exactly what Mr. Zaric said. He used all these words but in a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can clear that with him, just ask him to repeat his answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and also there is one more thing since I'm already on my feet, maybe I should draw attention of my colleague to this. Mr. Zaric here says on couple of occasions they were talking about this and unless Mr. Lukic would like to clarify that, the words that were used for people who are to be exchanged, it seems like here what I see in the transcript that those words were used by Mr. Tadic, Cancarevic and Todorovic and this is not what Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we have the answer clarified, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were mentioning the conversation with that police officer for whom you said that you only saw him there as being a private police officer of Mr. Stevan Todorovic, tell me, who was talking to him, who was having an argument?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Tadic and myself, on the checkpoint in Gorice when he stopped all the buses and he did not allow because Grga Zubak -- he asked Grga Zubak to come out of the bus and to return him. We opposed to that and fortunately, I believe that in the end it all turned out to be well, but I remember very well this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: And when I talked about privately, that it was -- I thought that that checkpoint in Gorice, because Gorice is situated in the middle between Bosanski Samac and Brcko, there was a point which was used by Mr. Todorovic for various deals, he was implementing his own policies there, and for instance, talking about that checkpoint through that police officer whom he called kum, there were names of the people who were to be arrested and I talked about it when we had a meeting in Belgrade, and this is why I say that that checkpoint was manned by a private police officer of Stevan Todorovic, because they were implementing all the actions that he was ordering them to do, and those actions were not humane, not professional and not correct. They were not police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will also need a clarification, when you were talking about Grga Zubak, you said they were using these people as points, what did you mean, exchange points?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Mr. Todorovic, who had an influence, a certain amount of influence, and not to say that he was one of the first ones but he was certainly among the people who were deciding who was to be exchanged or not, and when I was talking about points, it means that he thought that since Mr. Grga Zubak worked before as a professional police officer, that he had certain authority on the territory of the municipality of Samac, that he was a member of the Crisis Staff from the HDZ, SDA and so on and so forth, it was probably those were his criteria, he thought that for Grga Zubak he could probably collect some important Serbs on the other side, people who were detained or imprisoned on the other side and they were using the words points, that's why I said when they were using those words, is that this is an incorrect statement because we are talking about people who were in a situation that they were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. It's a kind of not so clear issue here on page 18, line 9 and 10, reading this particular part of sentence in particular it's private police officer of Stevan Todorovic, I believe that it is not a right sense that the words of Mr. Zaric were translated so maybe my learned friend can clarify that with Mr. Zaric because we heard something a little bit different, that private could mean that it's ordinary police officer in that term or -- I would like to clarify that, if it's possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please clarify, what do you mean by this term, "private police officer"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of a person who obeys all the orders and who carries out all the tasks that Mr. Todorovic gives him, and those tasks were not very professional. It was not humane, and there were incorrect actions but because Mr. Todorovic was the personification of such behaviour he was choosing people to man certain checkpoints, to do those chores and duties and this is why I call it private police officer, this is why I said that, maybe the term is not exactly precise but that's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please answer by saying yes or no, tell us if Grga Zubak was exchanged during that exchange and the principle one person for one person, tell us if you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I think that yes, this is what happened, the exchange was on a one-to-one basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you bear with me for just a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question stemming from my client. Do you know that the Vukovarcani had anything to do with those police officers, with respect to the events that took place afterwards in Sid [Realtime transcript read in error "SIT"]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I have a lot of reason to doubt and to think that there is a link between that checkpoint of the police in Gorice --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours by the way it is translated this question really doesn't seem quite clear. First of all, it -- the events that took place afterwards in SIT. SIT was referred as Samac textile industries here and Mr. Lukic was referring to Sid town in Serbia, so -- and when he said Vukovarcani this means people from Vukovar. And this would give sense to the question probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe he can repeat the question slowly, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am absolutely certain that Mr. Zaric will tell us about it if he knows about it. I have asked if there were some ties with those police officers, those officers that Mr. Zaric was describing as being at the checkpoint and he will -- and I mentioned the Vukovarcani inhabitants of Vukovar, and Mr. Zaric will certainly tell us what he understands, and yes, indeed, I was talking about Sid, it is a place in Serbia and I wanted Mr. Zaric to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a certain connection according to my very deep belief, and the link is precisely with this checkpoint of the police in Gorice that I was talking about. And what later turned into an incident when we arrived in Sid, in front of a motel, at a parking lot there. We arrived in the afternoon, late in the afternoon, two or three soldiers wearing the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army asked to see Mr. Grga Zubak. I don't know what happened. I was not there immediately at that point. I received that information only later on from Mr. Tadic and from the people who were providing security for this convoy. But I heard these three soldiers came up to the bus where Mr. Zubak was, they had this information and then a problem occurred, they started cursing his Ustasha mother, they wanted to get on the bus to pull him out of the bus and I believe that only thanks to the courage and the cold head of the people in the security at the checkpoint, a larger scale incident was prevented. When I say that there must have been a link, I can only assume that the people from the police in Gorice must have had some connections because I think that this policeman in Gorice came from that area and I'm sure that he had informed somebody that Mr. Grga Zubak was on that bus and maybe it was that group that was to do something to Mr. Grga Zubak and that's why I have established this link, because these people from Vukovar, these Vukovarcani did not have a way of knowing who the people on the bus was. Still they mentioned the name of Grga Zubak who had already been involved in the incident on that same way, and that is why I am of the opinion that there must be a link between that checkpoint and what had happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a short question suggested to me by my client. You've mentioned in your testimony Mr. Ante the veterinarian who was exchanged in Vemetin in 1992. That was not actually organised and had nothing to do with the Samac commission. A question from my client was: Are you aware that the family of Mr. Ante, the veterinarian, remained in Samac and they still live there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the fact. I know that the son of Mr. Ante, the veterinarian and my son are good friends. And Ante's son has business premises not far from the centre of the town and I also know that the veterinarian's wife has kept her apartment and the family has remained there all throughout the war and they still live in the territory of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His wife is also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, she is a Croat. I believe her name is Zdenka but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we shall move on to another topic. Can you please repeat the lady's name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I believe that her name is Zdenka but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in the indictment, Miroslav Tadic is charged with a close cooperation with yourself within the framework of his role in the 4th Detachment. That is what the indictment alleges. It is not indisputable that both of you were members of 4th Detachment. Can you tell us something about your cooperation from the time the 4th Detachment was established to the moment when Mr. Tadic left the 4th Detachment and left for another post? What kind of a cooperation did you have, if any at all?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: From the 5th of January, 1992, when the commander of the 17th Tactical Group issued a decision that was Mr. Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, to appoint the command of the 4th Detachment, which -- in which both Mr. Tadic and myself had leading positions, Mr. Tadic was a member of the logistics and I was in charge of the security and morale, from that moment on, we had a bit more opportunity to see each other and talk to each other. I would like to say very honestly that Mr. Tadic was the least present during the conversations and the meetings of the detachment command. By the nature of his work in the logistics, he did not have to be present. And secondly, we respected Mr. Tadic as a person older than the rest of us and the commander did not insist on his presence because there was no need for him to be there. There were no particular tasks to be given to him. Therefore, there were no close connections between the two of us in terms of the organisation and the work of the 4th Detachment. Although some witnesses have tried to portray our relationships as being very close before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did Miroslav Tadic have any activities regarding the 4th Detachment before its establishment? You've mentioned meetings in November and December. Was he present at these meetings? Did he engage in any activities before the establishment of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. He had a marginal role, or no role at all. I did not see him at those meetings that we had before the war. Mr. Tadic was neither an officer nor a commissioned officer. He was not attending any of the meetings during which we discussed the topics that would have a serious security character.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And another question that is linked to some of the testimonies during the Prosecution case: Were you present or did you hear that a meeting was held or that an activity took place regarding the 4th Detachment in the AS cafe, if you did hear something, tell us what you heard.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: There was no meeting of the 4th Detachment in the AS cafe. What kind of a command would that be to allow itself to hold its meetings in a coffee place where there are other people as well? This is really ridiculous, it's farcical. It would be sad if it was not funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've heard testimonies of various witnesses here and I'm going to ask you directly: Did you hear, during the relevant period, that Mr. Tadic had problems with specials or volunteers or people in multi-coloured uniforms, the people who came from Serbia? Did you hear at that time anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that, and I know more about that than about other things, because of the posts that Mr. Tadic held after the outbreak of the conflicts. He worked in the civilian protection, and also he was actively involved in the exchanges, and they had their positions and all of that, and I believe that on several occasions he was exposed to humiliation and I remember very well one or two days when I returned to Samac, I don't know where I had been, but I heard that he had been ill treated, him and his son. He was forced to destroy some inscriptions from the previous systems, he had been threatened while he was performing his duties, and the threats were especially from Mr. Lugar. That was while he was performing his duties in the civilian protection. I also heard, I did not witness that, but I heard about the arrival of Zvezdan Jovanovic, who is now a media personality in Serbia, and many others, and that he had been humiliated by them and ill treated by them. I'm sure that Mr. Tadic was a person who would exploit -- expose to us all sorts of ill treatment by those people, people from Serbia, by those specials who had arrived from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned and we've also heard a testimony about Captain Jez, who was also a security officer, and you've mentioned him in that context recently. Can you tell us about the relationship between this man and Todorovic and his specials? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: A day or two days ago, I did mention Mr. Jez and I said unfortunately he was also a commander but that was very unfortunate. He was deputy commander and the chief of the security organ in the 2nd Posavina Brigade. To my mind, this person is prone to dodgey deals, prone to crime, very arrogant, very coarse in his behaviour, very ill mannered and had I not known that he had arrived from Banja Luka and had I not known that he was an intellectual because he has a bachelor's degree, he's an engineer, I would not have been able to believe that, I would have always thought that he had arrived with this gang of specials. He was a very ill mannered person, not mature enough for the post that he was -- that he held. However, we had to tolerate him for a certain period of time. Eventually he was arrested and luckily enough he left our area in the package with Crni, Lugar and all the other specials who were arrested in November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My next question arises from the testimony of my client, who has said that in the massacre in Crkvina and in the killing of Dikan he heard from you. Can you tell us how Tadic reacted when he heard about these two crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: His reaction was the one of deep distress, and as far as I can remember, he said that he was afraid that this would escalate and that we would not be able to control the situation, that he was deeply disappointed that something like that had happened, that he is now -- he is now afraid. I had told him some details and how I heard about it originally, how Mr. Lugar had killed these people, I did not want to tire the Trial Chamber with this, but obviously, Mr. Tadic reacted in the way I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions about the exchanges and about the money involved in that. We've heard testimonies about that. During your testimony, I understood that you had all sorts of intelligence about the events in Odzak and in Samac during the war. On the other hand, I concluded from your testimony that very many acquaintances of yours and relatives of yours were also exchanged. I would like to know before you appeared before this Trial Chamber, did you hear stories about bribes, money and exchanges and did you hear anything about -- in that context with regard to Mr. Tadic, that would concern Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Not a single word within that context. Throughout the war, I did not say anything that would concern Mr. Tadic [as interpreted]. The first information about that or insinuations or the formations I heard here during the various testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have some problems here in the transcript. I will read it out in English so Mr. Zaric will hear what it says and this was not actually his answer. Here on page 26, line 20 and 21: "Throughout the war I did not say anything that would concern Mr. Tadic." This is literally what it says in the transcript. And this is not what Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is obviously an error in the transcript. Can you please repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, for the duration of the war, while Mr. Tadic was most immediately involved in the exchanges as a member of that commission, I did not hear from anybody on one side or the other, and I had hundreds of conversations, that Mr. Tadic would take any money or bribe from anybody in order to do anybody a favour. Just on the contrary, my information about Mr. Tadic is just the opposite, it is all very positive. I believe that this arose from the testimonies of the witnesses who were prepared to say what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's not speculate. You said that you know -- have different information about Mr. Tadic. Do you know what his financial position was before the war and did he help people before the war?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The town of Samac had about 6.000 or 6.500 inhabitants. He was among the wealthiest people there. He had most money and most assets in the town, and he was recognisable as the person who very often, within his abilities, always helped other people. He always gave money to his friends and acquaintances who wanted to open their own private business or they needed to borrow money for festivities or other things. He was -- as -- an unofficial bank, and every time he lent money, he never asked for these -- from these people for any interest. He was one of those people who did not have any reason to target people who had to be exchanged, and ask them to give him money for favours. This is my very deep conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When he was lending money, did he lend money to everybody, irrespective of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: He gave money to everybody. I don't know for sure who these people were but it was a public knowledge that anybody who wanted to borrow money, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Roma, everybody could go to him, everybody could ask him and many people did indeed turn to him for loans, and it was nothing unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, a few questions that arise from the last answers to Mr. Pisarevic's questions, when he asked you about your acquaintance with those who are present here and who are not present here, you said something about Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Simic, but didn't hear anything about your acquaintance with Mr. Tadic. I did not hear your opinion of Mr. Tadic. I would like to hear primarily, based on your knowledge, your immediate knowledge, during the war, based on the facts that you witnessed and the facts that you heard, I would like to hear what you think about Mr. Tadic and his attitude towards other ethnic groups during the war? How did he treat Croats and Muslims? We've heard all sorts of testimonies but you were also an eyewitness to all that so can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, I knew Mr. Tadic when I was younger. He was one of the best athletes in our area. Later on I knew him as a very loved teacher at the school, and then I got to know him better during the war. In my eyes, Mr. Tadic is a humanitarian and a person who, with all his being, worked in this commission for the exchange, in order to help people, miserable people, that were exposed to all sorts of hardships by the war. I know from many stories, stories told to me by my friends who had left and my relatives who had arrived, I attended only two exchanges with Mr. Tadic, and I've testified about that, but I heard about many of his travels, many of his departures, from the people who arrived. I heard and I listened to their stories. The duties that he performed in the technical sense, I believe that he performed them with a lot of emotion and he invested a lot of his energy to help these wretched people as much as he could, and within that context, I perceived Mr. Tadic, and I've heard dozens of such stories about Mr. Tadic. And this is not an exaggeration. Whatever I said is not an exaggeration. I have another comment that I almost wouldn't like to volunteer. I was very surprised to hear the testimonies of some people, knowing how much effort he invested to help them. So -- but that is not important. What I have just said is my official opinion of Mr. Tadic, and I also know that as the commander of the civilian protection -- left right and centre exposing himself to danger in order to repair or rectify any problem that was the consequence of shelling, of killings. We have -- we faced with a bad situation because over 860 people were killed in Samac and we had over 130 civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Trial Chamber will be able to evaluate that. Can you please now answer my question with either yes or no? This is my last question with regard to his activities in the civilian protection and during the exchanges, what you saw, what you heard, did you witness any discrimination shown by Mr. Tadic towards any ethnic background, any other people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Never. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the testimony and the answers that you gave to Mr. Pisarevic, you mentioned an occurrence linked to the detention of 4th Detachment members to the Samac police station, and you also mentioned that the Commander Nikolic called Stevan Todorovic and Blagoje Simic in relation to these events, and you then spoke further, that Todorovic replied and so on and so forth. Do you perhaps recall what Commander Nikolic told you, what was the reaction of Blagoje Simic, what did Blagoje Simic say on that occasion, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, commander told me that Mr. Blagoje Simic said, first of all that he was surprised that there were members of the 4th Detachment who were imprisoned and he said that he had nothing against something being done or everything being done for these people to be released and he then pointed him to Mr. Stevan Todorovic as being the chief of the public security station, who would be -- who was the commander of the station, and that this was within Mr. Todorovic's jurisdiction. So this was more or less in a nutshell what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Further on, and I think that could be a minor interpretation mistake, but perhaps this is a good time to clarify it, on page 19570, testimony of the 13th of May, you spoke of the behaviour and the reactions of Dr. Simic at the meeting of the command regarding the document entitled information. You spoke briefly that Dr. Simic was a very calm, moderate, that he was trying to find common ground with the other participants, but line 12 of the transcript, on the page that I have mentioned, there is a sentence which is inconsistent with your testimony. I'm going to read it now, and I would like to ask you to clarify it, if need be. So this -- the sentence is the following: "He spoke about the relationship between civilian authority and military authority, the military organs, and then you said the following: [In English] "And then I was given the chance to react and I said that his words were too harsh, and that this is not what the army did." [Interpretation] So what I now and then found odd was that his words were too harsh. That is not consistent with the rest of your testimony. Specifically, could you tell what Dr. Simic's reaction was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that I used these words in this context. The only thing I said was that Dr. Simic expressed his dissatisfaction in his belief that the document entitled "information" had more politics in it than should be. That was his reaction and that was his comment of the information and that was his sharpest comment, and if I said that was the sharpest thing he said and if it was interpreted in this way, what I meant to say was that Dr. Blagoje Simic wanted to say that the information in some elements was very politically coloured and that was his sharpest criticism regarding this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now I'd like to go on to a line of questioning regarding the subject itself, although this is obviously -- the case itself, although this of course was connected. If you please, could you tell me if you and Dr. Simic, together, planned the forcible takeover of power in Samac before April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information or knowledge that Dr. Simic, together with the command of the 17th Tactical Group, before April, 1992, planned the forcible takeover of power in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I never had any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are a person who fulfilled certain posts before the war. I'm not going to repeat that. You are an experienced policeman so to speak. Security person. Security officer. Did you ever have any information in the course of 1992 and 1993 that Dr. Simic had ordered that somebody should be arrested in Samac or detained?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, never, never. I never received information that such a suggestion stemmed from Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that Dr. Simic, in the course of 1992 and 1993, had ever ordered beating up of people who were detained in some of the detention centres in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never had this information at hand, and I remember, in the autumn of 1992, if this deserves to be mentioned, when, as it happens, in one house belonging to Milan Milicic in Pelagicevo, who was celebrating his patron saint's day and he invited some people, and as it happened, I was there in that house, not knowing and even if I had known, this isn't so important now, Mr. Blagoje Simic came, Mr. Milan Simic, and Mr. Stevan Todorovic came, and there were a few other people that I knew, and in the meantime, there was a very fierce verbal argument between us, between Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic, and I remember when Mr. Blagoje Simic said to Milan, in a sense that he would -- it was never up to him, he was not supposed to do what he had done in the school. I remember that Blagoje said that but that was by the by for me to say that to Milan, since Stevan Todorovic and I always had arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, Dr. Simic condemned what Milan Simic did?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he condemned what Milan Simic did and I have to say that this was a bit of a surprise at this kind of meeting, because they met often, they socialised, they carried out this policy, so I thought that this was in these negative elements, they were far too often together, but really Mr. Blagoje reacted in this situation as I just mentioned, as I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, I presume that we will agree that those were members of the Crisis Staff, they were from different parties; is that correct, Mr. Zaric? They were people who were from the Reformist Party and liberals and from the SDS and there were non-party people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I was not involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Only if you know.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I did not -- I was not involved in this kind of analysis but according to the people that I know it is a fact that to start with not all the people were from the Serbian Democratic Party but very quickly, they accepted its policies, that is uncontested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on, when we are speaking about these relationships, Samac is not a very large town and you're a well informed man. Would you agree with me if I tell you that Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic were very close, also with respect to the way that they behaved, and also their view point on life? Would you agree with me in that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: They were, and in particular, this is where I found Milan Simic rather a surprise because I knew him from before, not in this context but later on he gained elements of a very rough Serb nationalist and he joined in certain actions with Stevan Todorovic, with getting drunk, having brawls, lecturing other people, trying -- being arrogant, trying to become a cult personality, these were the characteristics of both of these two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Milan Simic was president of the executive board, and I presume that you know, considering that before the war, you heard -- had certain -- you fulfilled certain functions in the municipal structures, that Milan Simic, within this function, he had access to important financial means and to the budget; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. He was the main man, as far as finances were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Stevan Todorovic had behind him his policemen and certain other personalities of dubious character?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you, as a conscientious person, as an officer, reacting to such occurrences, you condemned this link between capital and armed force, that is namely could you tell us if you know whether any criminal activities of these two regarding smuggling of oil, et cetera, cigarettes and drinks, everything that was lacking during the war, could you just answer with a yes or no because it's time for a break, if you have any information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have information and I agree with your assessment and I can give you more information regarding some things that I know more about, if you assess that this is relevant to speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is possible we will be speaking about this but it's now time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I had asked you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, earlier we spoke of the relationships between Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic, at the question of my colleague, Mr. Lukic, you also mentioned Captain Jez. Are we going to agree that detention and arrest of Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic by the military police was in fact caused by certain information in respect of their illegal activities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The reasons for their arrest, I don't know the exact reasons. They were detained and arrested by the organs of the military police, commanded by the security organ of the East Bosnia Corps but I cannot rule out the possibility that one of the reasons for the arrest of Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Simic, and before that, of Captain Jez, could be linked because of certain machinations that it could have been some kind of a link in respect of certain instances of criminal activities, of criminal offences, so this -- there could be some grounds for qualifying this in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The activity that was linked to the information, what we call the letter with 13 signatures, which is exhibit number 127, also speaks of an initiative which existed to call the session of the municipal assembly of Samac where the executive organs of the municipality would be critically looked at.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of the proposals defined in the conclusion after the information was discussed and on the 29th of November, when conclusions were adopted, when certain proposals were put forward, one of the conclusions was the suggestion to finally hold the first assembly session as the highest legislative body and that certain matters are resolved at this assembly, and that everything is cleared up at this assembly, and it was within this context that this proposal was put forward within the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you tell me if you have any personal knowledge, direct knowledge, that Dr. Simic ever took part in these illegal activities that we have spoken about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I have nothing I've heard against Dr. Simic but I would like to say to the Honourable Trial Chamber that when I was interviewed in 1998, when I gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, I didn't try too much to differentiate between the executive and the legislative power, I called it all authorities in Samac, and then certain hypotheses were weaved around these what I call the authorities. I didn't speak of Dr. Simic specifically or other structures but now, when through the practice and what I feel to be individual responsibility and how it should be considered, perhaps there is some need for somethings not to change my testimony, not to change my statement, but to point to how I perceived them now from the point of view of legislative and executive organs in the area of the municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when we are speaking about the legislative organ, we are talking about the municipal assembly of Samac, which is conditionally speaking legislative organ. We know that the municipal assembly in fact adopts drafts of the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Further on, to your counsel, you spoke about some threats by persons from the civilian authorities. First of all, did Dr. Simic ever threaten you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard that, nor did he ever personally -- did he ever express a threat in that context, or said anything that I should be fearing Dr. Simic for any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that before your commercial activities, economic activities, you were head of the secretariat for internal affairs, I think it was in the 1970s, I can't quite recall, but what I'm interested in whether you would agree with me if I say that the principle within the organ of the interior or internal affairs, what happens is that the municipal assembly proposes the candidates but the final decision and the appointment is done by the secretariat for internal affairs, that is the minister, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the way in 1975 I was appointed chief of SUP in Samac, and I don't think that this mechanism changed, not at the time when Mr. Todorovic was appointed, as chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we will go on to the subject in relation to Odzak. First of all, would you agree with me, with my assertion that in relation with the work obligation and we've already heard many testimonies in respect of this, but would you agree with my assertion that those people who went to the work obligation were Serbs, Muslims and Croats, that is regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were different structures but it was dependent -- it depended on the nature of the work that they were carrying out. I would say that certain harder jobs and -- that were more difficult jobs were done by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And we can also agree that a large majority of the Serb population was mobilised and they were on the front line, they were carrying out combat tasks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of the able-bodied Serb population, they were in military units and they were carrying out the hardest tasks in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have also heard the testimony that in the territory of the municipality of Samac, I think there were over 500 people who died; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was over 580 who were killed in the municipality of Samac were killed, 440 were soldiers from the army, and the others were from the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because of the shelling of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, because of the shelling of Samac and when we are speaking about the soldiers, many of them were killed on the defence line and most of them were killed precisely on that defence line of Samac by HVO forces because throughout this time, we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zaric, those of us here who come from the area of former Yugoslavia, we understand very well or more or less we understand well the category of social property, state property, and so on. That is however not the case with our colleagues who come from other legal systems. So I'd like to very briefly answer my question, would we agree that this concept of social property was practically present, it was valid, before 1992, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we are speaking about social companies, social institutions, et cetera. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Directly, this is not related to the case but I will ask you a question because there is an indirect link. Would we agree that the transformation of this property in Bosnia-Herzegovina in fact started after the Dayton agreement, in the sense of privatisation and the transformation of property, if you can just say if you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I think that some of it started happening before, but not in the sense of real transformation, the way it was carried out after the Dayton agreement, but the reform forces or reformist forces on the level of Yugoslavia that were led by the president of the executive council, Mr. Ante Markovic, and who were very much present in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in favour of market economy and the -- in the situation where workers would use their shares to buy parts of the companies, but I would say that this activity was interrupted by the war and, as you say, it continued or it resumed in the more serious manner after Dayton agreement, after the first preconditions were established so that something could be done properly in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But my point is the following: We agree, and we are speaking about the territory of the municipalities of Samac and Odzak. You know about the companies since you were in that realm of activities in the economy, we agree that these large companies were socially owned before the conflict erupted in April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is not contested, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the management of these companies, that was done by the social, political community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic tells me that this is a normal term in where we come from but perhaps we should clarify for the transcript, sociopolitical community, that means the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The municipality practically speaking was the lowest form of local sociopolitical community in -- within an administrative unit at the time of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And one -- some of the forms were socially owned; is that correct, these were large systems, state-owned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These were railways, post service, electrical supply industry and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that we have made this introduction, I would like to ask you to look at the exhibit, or rather several exhibits that we have tendered here and perhaps you can make some comments with respect to the situation in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have please Exhibit D12/2 and ter also?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You talked about the introduction of the military administration and we have agreed on the fact that the complete organisation of life, the movement and the functioning within the military administration was under the command of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have version ter in front of Mr. Zaric and English version of this exhibit to be put on the ELMO and our learned friend from interpreter's booth, they have already copies in order to facilitate translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, this is an exhibit that we've already discussed. This is a decision of the state of the Serbian Republic of BiH, 31st of May, 1992, and it talks about various problems, about the security, economy at the time. Mr. Zaric, tell us if at the time you had ever had the chance do see this document or do you see it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this decision. I believe that this is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Upon reading Article 1, you can agree with me that it speaks for itself and we will elaborate on it at a later stage of this trial. I wish to draw your attention to paragraph 1, when it says, "Those duties are carried out through the executive committee of the municipal assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is when we can read in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the English version on the ELMO for the benefit of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Then it talks about the various functions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes in Article 2 we can see which tasks are -- I can see what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the interpreters wanted to have the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I already provided them with two copies of English version. It's D12/2 but nevertheless, Your Honour, I finished it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will not go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Please leave that decision there for a few seconds and I would like us to talk about Exhibit [In English] D102/1 [Realtime transcript read in error "P102/1"], please. Just for the record, I said on page 42, line 18, my question was that actually I was referring to the various function of executive boards of municipality and government, in terms of protection of the industrial capacities. That was the basis of my questions?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, is it P102 or is it D102/1 because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's Defence, yes. It's Defence Exhibit D102/1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, I believe that you can read this, although the copy isn't exactly clear, but you can see that this is a document stemming from the Republika Srpska, dated 14 of July, 1992. This is an instruction on implementing the decree on the compulsory handover of spoils of war and spoils acquired by other means to the republican commodity reserves. This document is self explanatory. [In English] For the transcript I can suggest -- I'm not an expert in the English language of course but the terms spoils of war and spoils -- the sense is the requisition actually, the term requisition. It's more appropriate term, because I spoke, you know, a couple of months ago with the interpreters and they suggested me that it might be a proper word, but anyhow, I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is an official translation which has been before the Court for a long time which is translated as spoils of war, which is a commonly known term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If my learned friend wishes to have it retranslated or checked, nothing prevents him but this isn't the appropriate way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I actually will leave this topic to my final submission because we are professionals here. Maybe we should speak about the spirit of law and interpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Trial Chamber can only follow the official translation of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, in the second paragraph of this instruction, you can read that all movable property and assets should be handed to the government of the SRBH, and should be handed over to an authorised municipal or republican organ. Later we read that it is the military police that is taking care of the security. Then later on, in paragraph 3, we can read that it is the municipal organ for the economy and we see what they are in charge of. Paragraph 4 talks about the command of the army. Paragraph 5 on the other page talks about the municipal organ for the economy and the fact that it is required to provide adequate storage space. Point 10 we talk about the ministry of the interior and what their duties and chores are and so on and so forth. Before seeing this decision today, were you aware that there was such an instruction issued by the government?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I had never seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that in Odzak, you remained up until the month of September, 1992, if I'm not mistaken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed in Odzak until the 25th or the 26th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit D167/1, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, this also is an exhibit of the -- Defence and I would like to you look at the last page. We see it is signed by the Minister of Defence, Mr. General Subotic on the 10th of October, 1992. You were not in Odzak at the time, I understand. Were you aware of this instruction?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of this instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like the usher to help us with another exhibit. [In English] [Previous interpretation continues] ... /1 please. Just for the record, it's D170/1. Thank you.
