utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, this is a letter emanating from the army main staff of Republika Srpska, the document was written on 2 September, 1993. We are talking about the execution of an order, confidential numbered, order rather, 1085-4 by the republican directorate for the commodity reserve, regarding cattle feed and maize. The document is signed by Major General Djukic. I presume that you have never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That is correct, I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that all the activities in Odzak within the military authorities linked to the economy, were under the -- were subordinate to the headquarters of the Republika Srpska, the government of the Republika Srpska, as well as the executive organs of the municipality? Would you agree with me after seeing all these documents that we've talked about? Is that a logical conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I can say that for Odzak, and I can say that the military command had its say, the government, the military command, and they very closely worked with the president of the military council, Mr. Popovic, who then also very closely worked with the president of the executive board of the municipal assembly of Samac. That I know very clearly. For the other part of your question, I cannot give any answers but I cannot exclude the possibility that there is a logical link.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, I am affirming to you that a whole series of orders that we have just seen right now, for which you didn't know they existed were in fact the basis to regulate relationship that existed between the authority of Republika Srpska and the military organs. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon reading these documents, and from what I was able to write very quickly, it was written very correctly, but I am wondering if it was really applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours one small clarification for the transcript, just to give some sense to the answer of Mr. Zaric. Here it says and from what I was able to write very quickly, I haven't noticed that Mr. Zaric wrote anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It should be read, instead of "write" it should be "read." It's a slip of the tongue of Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That will be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric would you agree with me to say that within the military authorities in Odzak, the military organs were competent for the initiating of eventual legal proceedings in case they would find out that there was an illegal activity? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I also presume that you would agree with me to say that during the period where the military administration existed in Samac [as interpreted] or from Samac, the food was transferred to Odzak for the purposes of the civilian citizens, for the people who were coming back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The food was arriving from Samac and also I can tell you that very large quantities were arriving because it was the summer time and harvest had not been done yet. Most of the wheat had gone to the silos in Bosanski Samac and not only to Bosanski Samac, it also went to other parts. But I know that the wheat had been harvested according to an order of the military authorities, and it was distributed to the installations that were the closest ones, now I don't know if that's what you're calling republican [Realtime transcript read in error "recognise"] reserves but I know one part of the quantities of wheat went for Samac, another portion went for Odzak, they went -- stayed in the silos of Samac, of Odzak, I know that, but it is uncontestable that the executive board and the authorities of Samac were providing the citizens with food and it's the citizens who were in the territory of Odzak upon the return of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript, page 47, line 7, after the word "existed" it should be in Odzak, not in Samac. Because it relates to military administration. And then also intervention to the same page, and line 17, Mr. Zaric mentioned republican reserves, department for reserves actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, we don't have to go into such great detail. I'm now going to list certain activities by the municipal organs in Samac with regard to Odzak I'm going to tell you what was done there in order to establish normal situation and you will agree with me, we've heard a lot of testimonies, at the end of the day you were there. So this is what I was asking and I don't want to go into any further details. Can you please give me brief answers. Besides the food for the civilian population, you will agree with me that cattle fodder was transferred from Samac to Odzak, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oil was also transferred for the aggregates in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also the spare parts for the water supply in Odzak, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and also for the electricity network in the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also medical supplies, medicines, for the civilian population in Odzak, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And also types of seeds for the autumn sowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe this was a mistake or maybe I have misinterpreted your words. You mentioned that before the military administration was introduced, Colonel Simic came to the Hit plant, wasn't that maybe Gojko Vujnovic who was the assistant for Commander Talic for the civilian affairs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It is possible, I'm not excluding that possibility. I know that he was in charge of civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into any details of that. Mr. Zaric, you were telling us about the episode while you were in Belgrade. Who did you visit there, that was in late May or early June, 1992. Don't give us any great details obviously. You have mentioned that when you visited the command of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence, Stevan Todorovic said that this was some sort of his headquarters. Did you mean that he personally and closely cooperated with the people from the command of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence, that they would meet later, is that a good interpretation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a very correct conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And if you remember, Blagoje Simic, did he say that these were his friends, did he also express some sort of a relationship with these people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, Mr. Simic was introduced to these people for the first time. I did not have the impression that Mr. Blagoje Simic and Mr. Tadic and Mr. Tadic [as interpreted] knew these people. The only person who knew them was Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Zaric. Can you please slow down? We have been having problems with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Page 49, line 21, here it says, Mr. Miroslav Tadic and Miroslav Tadic -- Mr. Miroslav Tadic knew these people. Mr. Zaric mentioned Mr. Milos Bogdanovic. Just this name to have in transcript instead of mentioning Mr. Miroslav Tadic twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the other name was Bogdanovic. Okay, that will be accepted. Also, Mr. Zaric, please pause before starting to answer Mr. Pantelic, because I can here the interpreter literally running to catch up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now lets move to another episode, one that you also described, and that is a removal or the appointment of Colonel Djurdjevic, Mico Djurdjevic. We will agree that the competent superior command was the 17th Corps and that Colonel Dencic as the superior officer carried out or rather decided that Colonel Djurdjevic would be removed or replaced. I'm talking about the formal aspect of that decision.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: If we look at the decision itself, by which Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni was appointed commander, then it is correct that he was appointed by Colonel Dencic, who at that time was the commander of the East Bosnia Corps or the 17th Corps at the time. That was its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will also agree with me when I say that Colonel Djurdjevic was transferred to the first Brigade in Brcko. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He remained very short time in Samac and he was in charge of the -- on defence lines in the zone of the 2nd Posavina Brigade and soon after that, maybe a month later, but I can't tell you exactly, he was appointed a commander of the 1st Posavina Infantry Brigade with its headquarters in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know that during the war, Colonel Djurdjevic became the chief of engineers in the main staff of Republika Srpska? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that. He did reach that level and he became the chief of engineers in the main staff of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Obviously and you will agree with me that this is all within the military structure, the question of appointment and removal of officers that it is all a very legitimate and regular work within the military structures? Will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Let me just say that in Samac, he was not suitable for a commander of a brigade and still he reached one of the highest levels in the main staff of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, and I think it is not disputable, that he was an expert in his area, which is engineering?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was one of the best known experts before the war, in that area, and that is probably the reason why he reached such a high command position in the main staff of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are no experts. We cannot decide on the ways the army appoints people but you and I will certainly agree that there were -- there was a fighting in Samac area with very complex strategic and operative tasks, that there was fierce fighting, will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the territory of Samac, within that context, was one of the most complex theatres of war, and it required a lot of courage in order to preserve that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Lukic asked you earlier today about the decision, the alleged decision on isolation, a document that we have seen here but nobody so far has confirmed its authenticity. Mr. Zaric, can you please tell us whether the inhabitants of Samac, of Croatian background, were ever put to work in -- on vital objects or facilities in the town of Samac [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. This never happened, and the document that this -- the period that this document refers to, this never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will help my colleague. Mr. Pantelic, the way his question was translated says, "Were the inhabitants of Samac, of Croatian background were ever put to work in" and then "on vital objects and facilities in the town of Samac" and I believe this is not what the meaning of the question was. I believe that Mr. Pantelic was discussing some sort of human shields. This is not put someone to work on vital facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. My question was whether Mr. Zaric was aware of the fact that any of Croat citizens of Samac were put on the vital objects in Samac during the war. That's exactly the question that I posed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours what are vital objects?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which document is he referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I was about to ask what the meaning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe what you do, Mr. Pantelic, repeat the question in your language slowly. Then we can have the answer. Maybe that will make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, as I have said earlier today, you were answering my learned friend Lukic's question, talking about document P71. Now I'm asking you based on your knowledge and on your information, during 1992 and 1993, were Croat citizens of Samac ever put on key facilities in the town, just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagoje Simic ever mention to you that he had made such a decision or participated in the making of such a decision as we see in P71?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Blagoje Simic never -- has never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that bearing in mind the fact that there were several seals or stamps of the Serbian municipal assembly, we've heard testimonies to that effect during these proceedings, is it then logical to conclude that somebody abused this document, especially with regard to this document? Based on the fact that there were several seals or stamps?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. He's an experienced police officer and I'm just trying to see the logical conclusion of the facts and events that were -- these are the part of the evidence exhibited before this Trial Chamber. In that sense. Fact number 1 -- fact number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe if the question was put another way I wouldn't have a problem with it. Just the way it was posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, would you please sit down? The witness can only answer as to what he knows, what he saw or what happened according to his knowledge. This is a conclusion you are trying to make him or you are putting to him without any basis at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, bearing in mind the fact that we have heard during several testimonies that there were several stamps of the municipal assembly, you as an experienced person, can you maybe draw a conclusion that it is possible that there may have been an abuse? I'm not asking you to speculate, I'm just asking you whether this is a logical conclusion, that there may have been the abuse of a stamp? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that somethings like that happened but it is also true that there was isolation, that there were people in isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are making my job difficult all the time. I'm just asking you to answer a question, the Defence has the right to ask leading questions in the cross-examination. Please just answer my question with yes or no. Don't add anything. And thank you in advance for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just going back a bit, that question which I sought clarification of, it's just gone off the screen again I've been trying to get up for the last few minutes, the question which was translated, sorry, the translation of the question was were people ever put on key facilities in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean that question regarding the people of Croatian nationality, whether they were put on vital facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's were they put on vital facilities. It's a meaningless question and Mr. Zaric said no, meaning, I don't know what putting people on vital facilities or sorry, he said key facilities, means. The document refers to isolation. I mean perhaps it could be put again properly according to what the document actually says and Mr. Zaric can give an answer based upon his knowledge and explain his knowledge. Otherwise it's just fairly meaningless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps you can clarify that during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the basis -- my learned friend, you will have enough time to clarify it. You have a key witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now I'm lost, Your Honour, I don't know what was my last question, thanks to the intervention. Could I have a second just to check the transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, I assume we will also agree that Croats and Muslims in the stadium in Crkvina in mid-May stayed for a few days, not longer than that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that but I didn't see it, but I did hear that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then a certain number of them were returned to their own apartments and houses and the others, I'm referring to men, were transferred to the elementary and the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. They went back to the sports halls of these two schools in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the signature on that decision is by Dr. Simic, and you couldn't say that for a fact, you're not a graphologist?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I can't say that for a fact, but from what I remember, from 11 years ago, and the way this document looked to me, and based on that memory, that's what I said, but I cannot confirm for a fact and I can't say with 100 per cent certainty that this is indeed Blagoje Simic's signature. If I could have a better version of that document, maybe I would be able to tell you more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you're not a graphologist, are you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not an expert in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is P what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: P71, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I'm going to put something to you, the way I see things, as Defence counsel. We have evidence that an attack on Serbian soldiers, who were on the bus, took place. We also have evidence to the effect that this attack was carried out in the area where Croatian inhabitants lived and we also have evidence to the effect that these Croats were armed. We also have evidence that a police operation took place by which civilians were transferred to the stadium in Crkvina. I'm putting it to you, Mr. Zaric, that this operation was under the authority of the military and police organs, and that it was a response to the incident which had taken place in the area of combat activities. Would you agree with that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, but as for the military organs, the 4th Detachment didn't have anything whatsoever to do with all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with you because I never mentioned the 4th Detachment, and I thought that this went without saying. As regards Exhibit P127, the document showing 13 signatories, would you agree with me if I said that, based on this information, an initiative was initiated by a number of deputies of the municipal assembly of Samac to convene a session of the assembly? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that this had such a positive effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me if I said that this initiative came from the deputies who were contrary to the book of rules of the municipal assembly, tried to convene this session in a coffee bar, among them Tubakovic, Stanisic and others, and also that that group did not achieve a quorum and could not make any decisions on anything and especially not on the issues relative to this information? Would you agree with me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But do you then agree, and you have already testified to that effect, that after that, a legal session of the municipality of Samac took place and that the things from that information were on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that that -- this session took place because I also attended that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that it was the wish of the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, as well as your own wish, for the army which interfered in some policies [as interpreted], wanted to carry out a putsch against the legally elected organs of the municipal assembly, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: This is a fabrication, this is nonsense, this has absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, I'm no specialist in the English language but on page 58, line 4, there is the word "policies," should it perhaps be "politics"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, thank you, I'm grateful for your intervention. In fact that was the politics actually related to legally elected organs of Samac municipal assembly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I clarify something here? The question was a putsch against the legally elected organs of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand what a putsch is. But I don't understand is it the case that there was a legally elected municipal assembly that you're putting to the witness and some one was attempting a putsch against a legally elected municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's the fact. That's not only the Defence case, that's a fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end, Mr. Zaric, I have a series of questions. According to the very precise instructions of my client, Dr. Simic, but before that, I'd like to ask you, you spoke of an event when your mother was moved out, was expelled, from the apartment. I spoke to my client. I called the field, that is Samac, and I was told that something in relation to this did happen but that happened after the Dayton agreement. Now, could you go back to that time and can you tell us when did that incident, this episode happen with the apartment and your mother? Was that something that happened in 1995, 1996?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: This happened in November, 1992. And not after the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I put it to you that this was outside of the framework of the indictment, and this was in relation to the session of the executive board of the municipal assembly, and practically, part of that executive board which was to do with the housing facilities. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No it was the session of the War Presidency and Mr. Blagoje told me decisively that the decision of the War Presidency four to three [Realtime transcript read in error "423"], that my mother should be moved out. No it was not the decision of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suggest a correction to the transcript, page 59, line 14, it's not War Presidency 423, it's voting four to three. Four votes in favour and three against. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it's supposed to mean actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My client, Dr. Simic, states decidedly that the Crisis Staff of the Samac municipality did not take any decision regarding the military action between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992. Do you agree with this claim?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I said how and from whom I found out and who told me this. I was not a witness to the making -- taking of this decision but the Crisis Staff -- that the Crisis Staff had taken this decision, I heard that from Lieutenant Colonel commander of the 17th Tactical Group and it was on the basis of this discussion of this interview, that's what I claim and that's what I'm claiming here before this Trial Chamber. I was not at this session and I did not hear of this decision being made but this is how I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My client, Dr. Simic, claims that he did not make a phone call to Commander Nikolic in the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Are you prepared to change your earlier testimony, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you're asking me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My client, Dr. Simic, claims that the Crisis Staff, he had personally never taken a decision or that he was ever in charge of appointing or dismissing any commander in the territory of the area of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Do you agree with this position or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he was not in charge of that but he influenced this policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic further claims that he never spoke to General Mladic on the phone, in Belgrade, at the command of the RVPVO. Are you ready to accept that claim?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. He did have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My client, Dr. Simic, claims that this meeting at the command of RVPVO, Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, did not attend. Do you agree with this claim?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. Frenki was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, never mind. We'll have to ask Frenki directly then.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Very well. You can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My client, Dr. Simic, claims that in the territory of the Odzak municipality, there was no organised looting by the civilian authorities, but that there were individual cases, certain individuals, who were under a completely different jurisdiction. Do you agree with this claim?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on, Dr. Simic claims that there was never organised looting by the civilian authorities, by himself personally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he did not do it personally but there was organised looting in my opinion. The way that I perceived the problem at the time. I don't think that he personally looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on, my client, Dr. Simic, claims that the volunteers from Serbia were never under the command of the civilian authorities in Samac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Simic excludes from that the public security station, then I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Simic claims that in the territory of the Samac municipality, there was never organised Serb Territorial Defence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. There was a Serb Territorial Defence, and how organised it was, that's another question, but it existed, it was there, as a legitimate institution, and not just in Samac, but in the entire territory of the Republic of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, before we finish, do you remember perhaps from conversations or perhaps you heard, that at the time when the president of the executive board was appointed, Mr. Milan Simic, Dr. Blagoje Simic was against his appointment but he was in favour of the appointment of Mirko Lukic? Did you about that? Did you hear that from anyone?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I heard this story at the time of the testimony of Mr. Blagoje but at the time, I was not aware of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on, Dr. Simic claims that the information of the 13 signatories document P127 is -- mostly does not correspond to the truth, that on the basis of this document, there was not a single criminal report that was ever filed. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: A large amount of my honesty and humanity, I entered into this information regardless of what Dr. Blagoje Simic thinks of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Zaric, I'm asking you these questions on the strict instructions of my client, so please don't think that I am trying to open any kind of debate on the subject. This is part of my job and I'm trying to do it as much as I can but thank you for your understanding. Further on --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I understand you fully but I'd like to give an answer which corresponds to the nature of the question that is asked. I'm trying to behave in an appropriate manner as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. I didn't have any other opinion on the subject. Of course there is no problem. Further on, Dr. Simic claims that this information, the military command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade and the higher command, the higher military command, that is the East Bosnia Corps, rejected it, rejected this information, in respect -- with regarding to political implication and the influence of politics on the army but they did undertake some measures regarding the arrests of those who were under suspicion of having committed certain criminal offences like Lugar and others. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, they never degraded this information in this context but I do agree that it was used also for certain arrests later on and it was also used to control the public security station, which was the subject of testimony of Mr. Slavko Paleksic and I presume that this was the basis for finally looking at what was going on at the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could I have just a few seconds to reorganise my papers? And I will almost finish the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am finished with the cross-examination of Mr. Zaric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I start, could I just say something in relation to the Prosecution's interpretation of Rule 90(H) and putting our case to a witness called who gives a contrary case to the Prosecution case? Your Honours will have heard over the seven days in which Mr. Zaric gave his evidence in chief that his evidence conflicted in a number of ways with a large number of Prosecution witnesses. Often in small ways but others in larger ways. The Prosecution's interpretation of Rule 90(H) is that where it is an accused who has heard all the evidence and has had a chance to put his own version of those particular events doesn't necessarily require the Prosecution to put each and every aspect of its case where one of its witnesses has given a contrary version to the accused's. If the Prosecution -- if that is the -- that's the Prosecution's interpretation, and if that's acceptable to the Trial Chamber and the Trial Chamber will accept for the purposes of my cross-examination that Mr. Zaric will have -- Mr. Zaric's case is opposed to us on some points, thus relieving us from the obligation to put each and every single allegation, of which there are probably hundreds, in relation to everything, for example, Mr. Tihic said, Mr. Lukac, there are many witnesses, there are some things I would like to ask him about but in my submission, the Prosecution does not needs to take Mr. Zaric to everything. Otherwise, we will be here for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could have only one word to what Mr. Re said, our only concern is that if such situation occurs here, I don't want Mr. Zaric to be confused because when Prosecution -- well, all right, put some quotations or something that was said during the testimony of their witnesses, I would feel grateful if they put to Mr. Zaric who is the witness who said that because otherwise, I mean, we have been through most of the episodes that were mentioned which Mr. Zaric's name was mentioned, for some of the episodes we didn't find important of them to be mentioned in his testimony. As my learned colleague from the Prosecution said, this would take an additional time of at least two more days but some of these incidents we believe that by now most of the evidence in this Tribunal already covered some of these incidents but I just don't want Mr. Zaric to be confused in case the Prosecution puts some quotations before Mr. Zaric. This is the only position that the Defence of Mr. Zaric would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is quite sure that the Prosecution does not intend to confuse Mr. Simo Zaric. They are only concerned with whether or not every minute detail which appears to contradict which some of the Prosecution witnesses said should be put to Mr. Zaric. What the Trial Chamber would like to say to the Prosecution is that the Prosecution is aware of the important aspects of their case or salient features of their case which they in cross-examination they should concentrate on. The Trial Chamber has also observed that there are many, many details that have been given by Mr. Zaric perhaps in his effort to be thorough and also to feel he has completed his case which are not necessary in this case and which also are not contentious. It's really looking at the main features of the Prosecution case and then extracting that supporting evidence from Mr. Simo Zaric. Obviously, if you're going to quote any witness, you make sure that the quotation is correct so that the witness -- Mr. Zaric is not confused, as Mr. Lazarevic fears and he's not the first accused to be cross-examined any way. He's in fact the last one. So the Prosecution can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I thank you for your guidance, your direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I'm going to ask you the questions as briefly as I possibly can and I want you could concentrate on the questions and I know it's your own Defence and I know you've been wanting to tell your side for many, many years but please, you must listen to the question and answer it and please as precisely as possible. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On Tuesday, Mr. Zaric, -- when you finished your evidence you finished it with an apology, an apology for the sufferings for which you wished to express your sincere apologies for the sufferings of every witness who was a victim of the war went through. You said it was your sincere apology, and it was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The apology with the expression of sympathy for these victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your apology of course isn't only directed towards those who gave evidence, is it? It was for all victims of what happened in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because you heard these people, the victims, who were witnesses give moving and harrowing testimony of what they went through, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if any witness from Samac had come and spoken, if every witness had come from Samac and spoken, I would have spoken individually to every single one to express my sorrow with regards to what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course you heard these people, the victims, who were witnesses here, give evidence of arrests, detentions, beatings, murders, rapes, looting, and deportation. You heard their own moving accounts of what had happened to them and the people around them, didn't you? The people from your community?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you heard them give evidence of what is now popularly known as ethnic cleansing, didn't you? These victims, who were witnesses, who came to court?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard these stories, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And today, in your evidence, you even referred to helping what you called "miserable people exposed to all sorts of hardship" and people you referred to as "wretched people". Those victims who gave evidence and the people those victims spoke of, they were in that category, weren't they, of miserable people, exposed to all sorts of hardship and wretched people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in light of your sincere apology for what happened to all the people, to those people, the victims, the witnesses and the victims of the war and what happened, I'm going to ask you a few things. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in light of your sincere apology to these people, Mr. Zaric, you don't deny, do you, having heard their moving and harrowing tales of what happened to them, that many non-Serbs were persecuted in Bosanski Samac in 1992 and 1993? You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not denying that. It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You don't deny, do you, that hundreds of Muslims and Croats were arrested in Bosanski Samac, only based upon their ethnicity? You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not denying that. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you also agree that many of these people who were arrested based upon only their ethnicity were beaten and some of them tortured while in captivity? You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That's correct, it happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you don't deny the beatings and torturing were a form of persecution of these non-Serbs, unfortunate enough to be locked up against their will, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And similarly, you must agree, Mr. Zaric, mustn't you, that non-Serbs were murdered in Bosanski Samac in 1992 and murdered only because they weren't Serbs and murdered by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will rephrase it. You don't deny or you would agree with me would you not, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, that question, especially the latter part of it when you say murdered by Serbs is a bit, it goes beyond the circumference, because if you say murdered by Serbs, it's like all the Serbs. So if you can rephrase it and be specific, without including -- without meaning the nationality itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I entirely take Your Honour's points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I will leave that question. You don't deny, do you, that non-Serbs were murdered only because they were of a different ethnicity, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: They were murdered but whether that was exclusively the reason, I wouldn't be able to state 100 per cent but it is a fact that non-Serbs, some non-Serbs, were killed, in the area of Samac, that cannot be denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You can't deny that non-Serbs in police custody were murdered and the reason for their murder was because of their ethnicity, such as Dikan and Taser [phoen]? You can't deny that, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that now Mr. Re is calling Mr. Zaric to speculate. What Dikan had in mind, what Mr. Lugar had in his mind when he murdered that person, this is really something that Mr. Zaric cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is nothing wrong to the -- with the question. The Prosecution is putting to Mr. Zaric. Mr. Zaric can deny or agree or explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand the question, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understood. If I take that the relationship between Lugar and the one he killed, then I would agree with your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You don't deny either, based upon your sincere apology to the victims, that the Serb forces who took over and imprisoned these hundreds of Croats and Muslims in facilities in Bosanski Samac, inflicted cruel and inhumane treatment on them only because of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you don't deny that their confinement was under inhumane conditions and this was inflicted upon them by their captors only because of their ethnicity? You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I am not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also of course don't deny that Muslims and Croats were forced to do labour, forced labour, against their will, only because they were Muslims and Croats? You don't deny that either, do you, based upon your sincere apology to the victims who testified here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: For a number of people, I agree, generally speaking, I couldn't accept for a number of people in that context, I agree that they were exposed to work obligations, and I -- as you would use to forced work, forced labour, which was a lot harder than elsewhere in other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you don't deny, do you, that non-Serbs were forced out of their jobs only because of their ethnicity after the takeover, in light of your apology, you can't deny that, can you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that a large number of non-Serbs remained without a job, but in those circumstances, conditions of war, a number of -- a large number of Serbs were also without jobs. It was a new situation brought on by the war. And the assessment that this was only relating to non-Serbs could not be reflection of the real situation but it is a fact that many remained without jobs but of all ethnicities, factories ceased working and many other things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a quarter to 6, Your Honour, if this is the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 18.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In light of your apology to the victims who gave their evidence here and the other people of Bosanski Samac who suffered as a result of what happened during the war, in 1992 and 1993, you don't deny that there was a takeover on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, by Serb forces? You don't deny that and you apologise to the victims for that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I do not deny the fact that on that day, there was a takeover, but I wanted to apologise to the victims for what they lived during the war. It doesn't mean that the takeover had to cause casualties but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But as it did cause casualties, and a great many casualties, it inflicted a great deal of untold human misery, stories that will never be known, now that you know that, you apologised to those people for the takeover and all that occurred as a result of the takeover, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fairness to Mr. Simo Zaric, Mr. Re, he has explained in his earlier answer that the takeover could have happened but it didn't have to cause casualties, and also, the Trial Chamber is of the view that his apology is really in the general sense, it shouldn't be taken as an admission of the allegations against him. I think it's better to be fair to the accused along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In fairness to the accused I'm not suggesting that the apology is an admission but I'm asking him to explain his apology and whether it includes various --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I think in fairness to Mr. Zaric, let's leave the apology as he stated it. Just go ahead and cross-examine him without linking it to his apology. I think it's normal for him. He felt the way he felt and if you remember during the Prosecution case, almost at the beginning of the cross-examination of each Prosecution witnesses, apologies were offered by the Defence counsel on the instructions of their client. I think it's better that the Prosecution respects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've agreed there was a takeover, you agree that it was a forcible takeover, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Forcible takeover by armed Serb forces of an area which previously or at the time had a non-Serb majority, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: If you are thinking of Samac as a municipality, statistical data testify to that effect. The majority of the population was non-Serb on the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So the short answer to my question is yes, is it, that it was a forcible takeover by armed Serb forces of an area which statistically had a non-Serb majority at the time? Is your short answer to that yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, as far as you know, the non-Serbs living in Bosanski Samac on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, didn't want to be taken over by armed Serb forces, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The armed Serb forces then installed a Serb-only regime, didn't they, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that Serb-only or the new Serb regime took control of all the vital facilities in the Samac district, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I do not know what do you mean by vital facilities but that the complete control of power was in their hands, well, one part of the municipality of Samac, from an earlier period, that's the fact, but I know what I consider to be vital facilities in Samac myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I must confess I too have a difficulty with what vital facilities means and I thought that it might be a term that was commonly used but I won't use that one any more. I'll just confine it to total control of the municipality. Those armed Serb forces took control and installed a Serb-only regime which then took total control of Samac. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the witness in his answer already gave one part of municipality of Samac. This is what he said in his answer. So after that stating that it was the whole municipality, this is something different to what the witness gave as his answer. His previous answer. Here maybe I can clarify this. On page 73, on line 6, one part of the municipality of Samac. This is what the witness answered. And now again we are asking about the whole municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic, referring to Mr. Zaric's answer, page 73, lines 5 to 8, I don't find the answer that clear because he talks about one part of the municipality of Samac, from an earlier period. That's the fact. Frankly, I'm not too certain what that means so maybe Mr. Re can clarify that in some way for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but Your Honour I believe that I understand completely what is -- what was it about. We are talking about two municipalities here. The pre-war municipality of Samac and then the municipality of Samac, Serb municipality of Samac, that existed during war. And then we have a third municipality of Samac that became into existence after -- after the Dayton peace agreement, and all right. A little bit earlier. All right. I'm corrected by Mr. Pisarevic. Definitely what we know from the testimony of Prosecution witnesses is that some parts of the pre-war municipality of Bosanski Samac, such as village of Prud, then Domaljevac, Bazik and some other settlements inhabited by Croats, were actually never, never occupied by Serb forces, and this is the meaning of the answer so quoting him that whole municipality of Bosanski Samac and putting this to the witness is simply confusing him, because he was referring obviously to some part of pre-war municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation is I think in accordance with what the evidence has been and I think it's better to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, all I'm asking you is -- will Your Honours just excuse me for a moment? The question has entirely gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think what I was asking you a moment ago was that the takeover led by armed Serb forces installed a Serb-only government or regime which then assumed control of a large portion of the pre-war municipality of Bosanski Samac, and when I say control, I mean total control.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When you say total control is a disputable word. The portion of the municipality of Bosanski Samac which were held after the 17th by Serb forces was under the control of Serbs. Aside from one part of the former municipality of Samac, which was under control of the forces of the HVO comprised by the Croatian Muslim corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... according to what I heard that Mr. Zaric said on page 75 line 6: "When you say total control is a disputable word." He didn't say that. He said, when you said a large portion, it's a disputable word. This is what I heard that Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is when the Serb -- the armed Serb forces took control of those parts of the pre-war Bosanski Samac municipality, they installed their own regime and introduced and implemented a series of discriminatory policies against non-Serbs, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: This Honourable Trial Chamber has to evaluate if everything took place the way you're trying to suggest but the authorities are in the territory of the municipality of Samac, which was under the control of the Serb forces, which remained under the control of the Serb forces, took certain measures according to some regulations which were established by the Republika Srpska as the new entity. That is a fact. Now, if all these measures were such as you're saying, that's disputable. I believe that all the measures that were applied by the Serbian authorities did not have a discriminatory character.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not suggesting all of the measures but a little earlier before the break, you agreed with me that the arrests and detentions, the confinement in inhumane conditions and so on were all discriminatory or persecutory against the non-Serbs. You're not going back on that answer now, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I do not wish to go back to that but I wanted to give short answers to the questions you were posing, and I was expecting you to ask me what I think, and why those arrests took place but I'm not disputing the fact one single moment that those people who were detained were exposed to torture and to everything else that you've mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that the measures that -- I'm sorry, you said that they took certain measures according to some regulations which were established by the Republika Srpska as the new entity. Do I take it from that that you are referring to the arrests, the detentions, the beatings, the confinement under inhumane conditions, the torture? Are you saying that the new Serb authorities did that pursuant to Republika Srpska regulations or --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Regarding the official documents, ascertaining that, I have never seen emanating from the official authorities of the Republika Srpska. It is uncontestable that all the sufferings and all the crimes that you mentioned is something that happened on the municipality of Samac. I cannot confirm this because I have never seen a document of that kind that somebody from the top would give an order to perform arrest, to a rape, to kill, I have never seen such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you're certainly not aware of any punishment or inquiry being directed by the Republika Srpska organs of government in relation to arrests, torture, detention, beatings, of people only because of their ethnicity, are you, Mr. Zaric, that occurred in Bosanski Samac? You're not aware of that, are you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: During that first period, such an activity is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's because, Mr. Zaric, it just didn't happen, did it? The Republika Srpska organs of government just did not do anything to punish those who committed those terrible crimes in Bosanski Samac in 1992 and 1993, did they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I only know because I have heard, that a certain number of detainees who were in Bosanski Samac were sent through the military court in Bijeljina or were tried there and that some civilian military tribunals heard cases and persecuted people who committed crimes in 1992 and 1993, but I had not any particular knowledge of that. Maybe some things occurred for which I had no knowledge, but I do not know that anybody was doing anything in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, it was well known at the time that Crni and Lugar and the paramilitaries were responsible for the Crkvina massacre, wasn't it? If you want to give a short answer, you can give a short answer for that one.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I know for Lugar and another member, I cannot generalise because it was just a few people. I know that those two men participated in that massacre but I cannot say that generally speaking it relates to all the specials, because only two men committed such crimes, or Lugar himself, so one can put this crime -- link this crime to him. Whether Crni was there, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you went to Belgrade to speak to some very important people about this particular massacre --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but the answer was not properly recorded. Mr. Zaric said, as for Crni, I can confirm to you that he was a chief of Lugar. This is what he said, and here we said, whether Crni was there, I do not know and there was one sentence after that that wasn't recorded. Maybe this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's better that he repeats the answer. Then we get it all in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you please, possibly, Mr. Zaric, repeat the answer to the question? The question was -- my question was, it was well known at the time that Crni and Lugar and the paramilitaries were responsible for the Crkvina massacre, wasn't it? It just wasn't clearly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The crime in Crkvina was committed by Slobodan Miljkovic, also known as Lugar. This is the information that I had, and it is indisputable that he was a member of the team of volunteers which [Realtime transcript read in error "245"] was headed and brought to our area by Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni. And by that, he is also held responsible. So if that is the case, then obviously, you are correct when you say that these two men committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This number, I apologise, 245, on page 78, line 21, I don't know what it stands for and it is not what Mr. Zaric mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't mentioned so it's just one of those things that I think that popped up. You can continue, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Zaric, what I'm just asking you about quite simply is you know that the perpetrators of that massacre were never brought to justice by Republika Srpska authorities, were they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That is a fact, a fact that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's also a fact that Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Milan Simic were never brought to justice by Republika Srpska authorities for the horrendous crimes they committed in Bosanski Samac and admitted to before this Tribunal? That's a fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: They were never tried. No proceedings were ever instigated against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was of course a matter of common knowledge throughout Samac what had happened at Crkvina and what had happened in the detention centres, wasn't it? The arrests, the beatings, the tortures, the murders, it was common knowledge in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Maybe at the beginning, this information was available to fewer people, but as time went by, I believe that this information was available across the board to all of us who lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, in 1992, 3, 4, 5, 6 and so on, there has been a justice system with a police force, and functioning courts, in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, there has -- there have been such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And a massacre of 16 people is no small matter in any part of the world, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing that you know of prevented the civilian authorities or the military authorities at any time after the 7th of May, 1992, from investigating the Crkvina massacre and bringing to justice those responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I am objecting to one. First of all we have the date of 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. I really do. I really do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Why? Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That the massacre is Crkvina happened on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With respect, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Prosecution put their case to the witness. He can answer. You don't have to correct them. It's their case. Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, nothing that you know of prevented the civilian authorities or the military authorities at any time after May, 1992, from investigating the Crkvina massacre and bringing to justice those responsible for it, correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Whether the days following that massacre were conducive to start any proceedings, but that doesn't mean that proceedings should not have been started at some other time. There is no -- these crimes are not time-barred and the investigations are not time-barred, concerning the circumstances when this happened, and who perpetrated it and the fear that we all experienced at the time, I'm not sure whether this was not done only to cover up all that situation, but also because there was a fear amongst official and non-official structure linked to the behaviour of these people [as interpreted]. I agree with you that there is no reason for not instigating proceedings. However, the conditions immediately upon the perpetration of the crime were not conducive to starting the proceedings in a safe and legally regular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You -- Mr. Pantelic has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Page 81, line 8, Mr. Zaric did not say the following, "There was a fear amongst official and non-official structures linked to the behaviour of these people." He said, "Because of the behaviour of these people" so maybe we can clarify what these people are and because of the general state of fear due to the actions of this group of people. And this is a really serious mistake here on page 81, line 8, and I first of all would like that Mr. Zaric is speaking slowly, to help our court recorder and our interpreters, and also I know everyone of us are quite tired, it's at the end of the day, but I hope that our friends from interpreter booths will be a little more and better concentrated what was said here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you don't have to go that far. So far we've been receiving good services from the supporting staff, including the interpreters. It's just a question of asking the witness to repeat his answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric could I just ask you to repeat slowly, as slowly as you can, the bit of your answer about your perception of why the perpetrators of the Crkvina massacre have never been brought to justice by the Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I said that I don't dispute the fact that proceedings should have been started against Lugar and others who committed this crime but it is also my opinion that immediately upon this massacre, the preconditions were not created, there were not conditions for a normal legal procedure against them because many formal and informal structures, official and non-official structures, in the territory of municipality of Samac, were afraid of these people who were prepared to commit such a crime, and their behaviour even before Crkvina was very bad, and along the same lines but later on, I believe that these proceedings should have started to -- if for nothing else than for the government to save the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When I asked you a few moments ago about regulations or decrees emanating from the Republika Srpska, your answer was, "Regarding the official documents, ascertaining that I have never seen emanating from the official authorities of the Republika Srpska, it is incontestable that all the sufferings and crimes that you mentioned are something that happened." I just want to clarify something from your answer. Are you saying that you've never seen anything from the Republika Srpska in relation to discrimination amongst the ethnicities? Or were you saying something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I've never seen a single document that would directly instruct anybody to take discriminatory measures against non-Serbian population. Secondly, I was not in the position to be close to the authorities to see any documents, originals of those documents. All throughout the war I was just a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But -- you'd agree of course or you'd have to that a strategic objective of the Serbian people that was to "establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities" was of itself a discriminatory policy or document, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Truth be told, that document and those strategic goals within that context as they were expressed and passed allegedly by the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, I saw that for the first time here when I was brought to detention unit here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about when you first saw it, I'm just asking you to comment on my proposition that a decision sorry, "Decision on strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which says, "The strategic objectives or priorities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are to, 1, establish state borders, separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities," you would have to agree, wouldn't you, that that is a discriminatory policy passed by the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I remember this document because it was an object of the testimony by a number of witnesses. If I was to comment only this position that you have put forward, then one could conclude that it was politically inappropriate and that -- that it led to very severe consequences later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Like ethnic cleansing. That's what it led to, didn't it? Or persecution?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is something that was typical of the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including our Samac, where we were in some of the elements. I'm sure that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You agreed a little earlier that the takeover was a forcible takeover by armed Serb forces of parts of municipality. You'd also agree, don't you, that as a result of that takeover, the authorities or the new regime, allowed looting of the property of non-Serbs to occur, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Looting was for everybody plain to see and that is part of every war. There are a lot of crimes committed during the war. Amongst the troops and the civilians, there were individual cases of excesses and there was also some organised looting. That's what I would call it. In other words, looting and robberies were an integral part of what one may call the consequences of the war, that war that raged on the territory of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This organised looting was condoned by the new regime, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I saw certain things from my own perspective as a human being, and I gave them the name that I gave them. I don't know, and I didn't know then, that these negative phenomena were investigated. I personally did not investigate any case of robbery and I can't give you any reliable information that this was organised or backed by the authorities or whether it was an individual phenomenon committed by individual criminals. However, the way I perceived things, I perceived them as something that was generally happening and that's the way I explained it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, non-Serb property was looted, including dwellings, businesses, personal properties, and livestock, wasn't it, in 1992 and 1993? Just concentrate on non-Serb, if you please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It is correct that during this period and especially during 1992, the cases of the number of robbery cases increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, the question I was asking you was during 1992 and 1993, non-Serb property was looted, including dwellings, businesses, personal property, and livestock?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This indeed did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it was organised looting, some of it was organised looting by Serb forces in control of parts of the municipality. You agree with that, don't you? You've only got to go to P127, the 13 signatories, where you and the other members of the Posavina command referred to organised looting. It was the document you spent two months researching.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I did confirm that there was organised looting, there was also individual looting. I don't know what else do you want me to say to fully answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know, this organised looting of non-Serb businesses, dwellings, personal property and livestock was directed at the property of non-Serbs because they were non-Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I know that most of the assets plundered by non-Serbs, but there was also looting by some abandoned Serbian territories, so it is not disputable that most of the looting was done in the villages abandoned by non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The looting, the organised looting, by Serbian authorities or Serb authorities was directed at non-Serb -- or sorry, property owned by non-Serbs because they were non-Serbs. That is, it was an ethnically based looting, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: A crime does not have borders of that sort. When I spoke about plunder, I was speaking about Odzak municipality. I had a very decisive opinion about that. I even gave you some examples to illustrate that. Maybe it would be good to look at this thing separately, and to look separately at the municipality of Samac and the municipality of Odzak. I remember that this is exactly what I said to your colleagues investigators, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We may come back to that at some other point. I just want to ask you about the people who were living in pre-war Samac and you've already said that there was statistically a non-Serb majority at the time of the takeover. You don't deny, do you, that women and children and elderly people were moved from their homes and villages by force, intimidation and coercion, those people were non-Serbs? You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't deny that, but those who left, they did not all leave by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. There were a number of ways people could leave Samac during the war. People could swim across the river, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the ways but they could also go to the Red Cross, they could register there, and they could express their wish to leave. That was another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, they could also get themselves some false identity papers and go off through Serbia. That was another way, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, the people who were held for long periods of time in the schools, or the SUP or the TO, and subjected to extremely inhumane conditions, who were offered the chance of leaving by exchange, you don't suggest that those who went by exchange were leaving voluntarily, do you? Having heard the evidence of the victims and witnesses who testified here about the reasons they left Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about this group of people, and between -- when one is between a rock and a hard place, I believe that they left for these reasons, as you have just mentioned. If I had been in their shoes, I would have left as well. That's how my relatives left Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And because their arrest and detention was only on ethnic grounds, their reason for leaving assisted by the Serb authorities was also on ethnic grounds, wasn't it? Maybe that question is not very clear. If I could perhaps rephrase it. What I'm saying is you've already agreed that the arrest and detention of hundreds of people occurred only because of ethnicity. The people who you've just agreed left because they were between a rock and a hard place, they left with the assistance of the non -- Serb authorities. One of the reasons the non-Serb authorities assisted them to leave was on ethnic grounds to remove these people from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The reason why people were detained, whether I agree with that or not, was not only because they were Croats and Muslims, but also because many of them possessed illegal weapons, and before the beginning of the conflict, they belonged to paramilitary formations such as the HVO and the Muslim forces, and they showed hostility towards the Serbian people, and this is an indisputable fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just go back to what I was asking you, and that is this, the people who were arrested and detained, you've already agreed were treated and subjected to the most inhumane conditions, whatever crime they may have committed, and you've agreed they were Muslims, predominantly Muslims and Serbs [sic], and the people in the schools were given a choice of going to an exchange and leaving or remaining behind and being subjected to discrimination that was occurring. In those circumstances, their leaving wasn't voluntary, was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that you have mentioned that Croats and Serbs were detained or Muslims and Serbs. The persons who were detained were Croats and Muslims. That is one small correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm corrected. I meant Croats. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: And as -- yes, you meant Muslims and Croats. I agree with you that they did not leave of their own will, that it was not their whim to leave Samac. They left because of the conditions that they were subjected to, they were detained. Let's put aside whether they were responsible of any crimes, but in light of the treatment they were subjected to in the detention centres, I agree that the best choice for them was to leave this area. Those who decided to remain in Samac later on were not exposed to any discrimination or to be more precise, I don't know of any such case, and that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But those who left, as you have just said, because of the conditions they were subjected to and their detention, and their best choice was to leave, you agree that the circumstances of their leaving was discriminatory, wasn't it? This forcing, this lack of choice, that was discriminatory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I believe that while they were detained, they were subjected to all sorts of discriminatory methods, they were beaten, they were exposed to all sorts of suffering, they were not given enough food and so on and so forth. We've heard testimonies here that I don't want to question because I did not participate in any of the exchanges, and I did not talk to the people who were given the opportunity to say during the exchange whether they wished to return or not. They were asked what they wanted to do and they expressed their opinion, they expressed their wishes. As a human being I understand the reasons for which many of them did not want to go back. I absolutely appreciate the reasons for which they didn't want to go back.
